blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Multilingual pipelines such as FineWeb2 apply one recipe across a thousand languages, leaving the failure modes of individual languages unanticipated. We use an LLM once, as a corpus debugger rather than a classifier: a tool-using agent explores the corpus through a read-only, budgeted API and compiles each finding into an executable test, which a native speaker then validates. On the 26.5M-document Slovak portion of FineWeb2, three runs costing \$2.21-\$2.84 each found seven findings over four phenomena. The largest is a machine-generated content farm of 1,408,437 documents (5.32%) that passed the pipeline's filters, 86.6% of it passing even stricter thresholds. Blinded labels support 6 of the 7 findings (defect rates .53-1.00 against .08 in a random control) and do not support one. The compiled suite scans the full corpus in 0.7 s of wall-clock time without a GPU, against \$12k-\$90k per LLM classification pass. The best static sampling baseline validates more selectors than any agent run, at under half the cost. The agent contributes exact prevalence, a precision estimate checked against sampled documents, an account of why the pipeline missed each slice, and a reusable test. We release the framework, Slovak test suite, validation data and agent trajectories.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Pretraining corpora are now built by pipelines rather than by hand. FineWeb2 ( Penedo et al., 2025 ) derives more than a thousand
language-specific corpora from Common Crawl with one configurable recipe. That
uniformity is what makes such resources feasible at all. One pipeline, engineered
once, yields data for languages whose communities could never afford a bespoke
crawl. It is also a structural blind spot, as the FineWeb2 authors say
themselves. Their language identifier confuses closely related languages, and
they could not test each language individually, so they ask users to review the
filtering for the languages they care about. Their one mechanism against
cousin-language contamination, a high-affinity wordlist filter, is applied only to
languages whose measured contamination exceeded 10%, and not to a mid-resource
language like Slovak with a large, closely related neighbour.

blocks.en:
Reviewing a pipeline for one language is exactly the work that does not scale.
Its established form is the manual audit ( Kreutzer et al., 2022 ; Caswell et al., 2020 ) , which is
invaluable, and recent single-language audits still pay off ( Signoroni and Rychlý, 2026 ; Tatariya et al., 2026 ) . But an audit is a
one-shot artefact. It describes a corpus at one point in time, does not compose into
machinery that can be re-run on the next crawl, and consumes expert attention
linearly. The alternative, running an LLM over the data as a classifier, turns a
curation problem into an inference bill and still explains nothing.

selector, a prevalence measured on the whole corpus, and a precision for human

blocks.en:
We frame an LLM, used once, as a corpus debugger whose output is a test rather than
a label or a data-selection policy. We build a reusable audit environment (DuckDB
over Parquet, eleven read-only budgeted tools, a finding schema) with a FineWeb2
adapter, and an agentic auditor that runs inside it under a fixed inspection budget
and a prompt that names neither a defect nor a neighbouring language. Around it sits a
three-stage workflow (discovery by the agent, validation by a native speaker,
deployment by a test runner with no model) in which validation can fail a finding.
It failed one of our seven findings, which comes out at a .07 defect rate and ships
flagged. Our audit of Slovak FineWeb2 yields seven findings over four phenomena with
exact corpus-wide prevalences and blinded human precision (Table 2 ),
among them a 5.32% content farm that the pipeline’s own language, duplication and
auxiliary-LID signals do not filter, and a language_score invariant that
fails in 11 of 12 FineWeb2 configurations. A per-run budget-matched
comparison against four static selection strategies shows what the agent does and
does not buy. It validates 2–3 selectors per run against
2–4 for the baselines, so the best baseline finds more than any agent run, and each
phenomenon it validated also lies within reach of a static strategy, although for
the adult spam we analysed that strategy’s sample without running the model on it (§ 5 ).
Its contribution is the measurement, the characterisation and the test. Finally, we release the Slovak
regression-test suite, the patcher that turns it into a drop list, and the agent
trajectories (Table 1 ). Every defect we report is a residual of an
already heavily filtered corpus, and several are visible only because FineWeb2
publishes rich metadata.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
FineWeb2 ( Penedo et al., 2025 ) extends the FineWeb recipe ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) to over a thousand languages using
GlotLID ( Kargaran et al., 2023 ) with a per-language confidence
threshold, Gopher- and FineWeb-style quality filters, and global per-language
MinHash deduplication with rehydration. Earlier multilingual web corpora ( Ortiz Suárez et al., 2020 ; Xue et al., 2021 ; Conneau et al., 2020 ; Kudugunta et al., 2023 ; Nguyen et al., 2024 ; Burchell et al., 2025 ) share its architecture and
its exposure to the LID error that Caswell et al. (2020) and Burchell et al. (2023) document. Audits of such corpora are an
established genre, covering 205 corpora by hand ( Kreutzer et al., 2022 ) ,
one English corpus in depth ( Dodge et al., 2021 ) , non-English
Wikipedia ( Tatariya et al., 2026 ) and Lombard ( Signoroni and Rychlý, 2026 ) . The WaC community studies the same
failure surface from the pipeline side ( Jakubíček et al., 2020 ; Barbaresi and Lejeune, 2020 ; Laippala et al., 2020 ) . We are downstream of these, asking how an audit
can be made repeatable and executable. For Slovak, cleaning practice is
established ( Pikuliak et al., 2022 ) and Czech/Slovak is a known hard
case for language ID ( Tichý and Libovický, 2026 ) . Sub-percent contamination still means
hundreds of millions of tokens ( Blevins and Zettlemoyer, 2022 ) , though we
promise no downstream gains ( Artetxe et al., 2022 ) .

blocks.en:
CheckList ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) argued that behavioural tests expose
model failures that aggregate accuracy hides. We make that argument for corpora,
and borrow the pattern of declarative data-quality assertions run on every build ( Schelter et al., 2018 ) , except that here the assertions must
come from people who know the language. LLM agents have been applied to
corpus-linguistic discovery ( Yu et al., 2026 ) and to the curation loop, where Kang et al. (2026) find
that coding agents optimise data-selection policies but tend to tune variants of a
known policy. Ours optimises no downstream metric and outputs a test suite instead of
a policy. We do not claim that LLMs are good language classifiers. The agent
writes the tests that label the corpus and never labels it itself.

blocks.en: 3 The Audit Environment
blocks.zh: 3. 审计环境

blocks.en:
The adapter exposes a corpus as two DuckDB relations over Parquet. corpus_meta has one row per document without text and serves exact
corpus-wide prevalence, while corpus is a deterministic 1-in-13 subsample
with text (2,034,894 documents) for whenever reading is needed. That split keeps
the environment interactive, because metadata aggregates over 26.5M rows return in under a
second while scanning 100 GB of text does not. The columns are the corpus’s own
metadata (URL, crawl, date, the pipeline’s language and language_score , minhash_cluster_size , the profanity-list count n_bad_words , the GlotLID top_langs distribution, and the
fastText, langdetect and Lingua predictions added by the ivykopal/fineweb2-slovak release), plus language-neutral derived columns
(domain, size counts). Nothing in the schema names a language pair or a failure mode.

blocks.en:
The agent acts through eleven tools, each listed with its budget cost in
Appendix A . They cover aggregation, sampling and single-document
inspection, text search, host and crawl statistics, sentence-level language
identification, two tools that measure and sample what a candidate rule selects, and save_finding . Aggregation is free, whereas every document read costs one inspection from a fixed
budget, charged once per distinct id. Every call is logged to a JSONL trajectory,
so an investigation can be replayed.
The free aggregation tool did not stop a query from returning document text, for
example substr(text, 1, 120) grouped and counted, so text could in principle
be read without spending budget. We checked every logged aggregate call. In the three
protocol runs none returned document text: the queries that touch text return
counts only. The fourth run in Appendix K returned text fragments in
three calls, the most frequent 100- and 120-character document prefixes and extracted
e-mail strings, and its inspection count therefore understates what it read. Later
versions of the environment refuse such queries.

blocks.en:
The agent runs one long trajectory in which it orients on statistics, forms a
hypothesis, retrieves evidence and counter-evidence, refines or rejects it, measures
prevalence, synthesises a selector, checks its precision and records a finding. Its system prompt
(Appendix B ) states the tools, the finding schema and the
epistemic standard (systematic, reproducibly retrievable, grounded in inspected
documents, quantified), and asks for calibrated precision estimates and
counter-evidence. Because it does not name any defect, failure mode or neighbouring
language, discovery stays attributable to the agent.
Appendix C verifies this mechanically and states exactly what the agent was told. We run it through the Claude Code CLI with only the audit tools and Claude Code’s tool-schema lookup enabled, and no shell, file or web access.

blocks.en:
The workflow has three stages with different actors and costs
(Figure 1 ). Discovery is where the agent works, and it produces
candidates. In validation a native speaker labels a blinded sample of each
candidate’s documents, after which a model tabulates that evidence and proposes a verdict
per candidate group that the annotator adopts or not (§ 4 ). Deployment runs the resulting tests without any model. Each test is a YAML
file carrying its selector, an assertion about future corpora and its evidence
(Appendix L ), and a status: accepted when the blinded labels
support it and the adopted verdict approves it, candidate otherwise. A suite
is a directory of such files, executable against any corpus implementing the adapter
interface.

All seven selectors are metadata-only, so the suite is exact over the full corpus.
It runs over all 26,470,482 documents in 0.7 s of wall-clock time on one
machine (about 13 s of CPU time across 20 cores), without GPU
or LLM calls. Classifying every document with the same model instead costs
$3.42 per thousand documents, measured on 400-character snippets batched twenty
per call. That is $90,456 per pass, or $12,309 at raw token prices without
harness overhead, and it recurs every crawl. The comparison is not like for like. The
tests are cheap because they reuse columns the pipeline and the redistributor already
computed in corpus-wide passes (language identification, auxiliary identifiers,
profanity counts, MinHash clusters), and a selector over raw text would cost a text
scan. The LLM writes the test once, and that test runs at scale.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
An LLM agent audited Slovak FineWeb2 for $2.21–$2.84 a run. It found,
measured and characterised slices that a native speaker then confirmed, and left a test
suite that runs without a model. It validated fewer selectors per run than the same
model reading a well-chosen static sample, and every defect it validated was within
reach of one static strategy (we did not run the model on the profanity-ranked sample
that reaches the adult spam, § 5 ). The contribution is the
workflow, which turns a one-off audit into executable, validated tests and can fail a
finding, as it did for one of ours (shipped as a candidate). It already runs
on eleven other FineWeb2 configurations (Appendix E ), and another community can point the adapter at its
own corpus and run the suite.

blocks.en:
This study covers one language, one corpus and three runs of one
model. Agentic discovery is shown only on Slovak, and the other languages in
Appendix E only re-ran tests written for Slovak. A fourth,
stronger-model run reproduced the largest phenomena outside the frozen protocol, but
its extra findings are unvalidated. The agent used 58–66% of its allowance.

blocks.en:
Human validation covers 255 documents labelled by one
native speaker (12–21 per finding, median 19), which
limits precision estimates and gives wide intervals. Labels were collected in two passes, and the criterion for unusable text was clarified between them: a fluent page that exists to place links or keywords counts as junk. 117 of the 255 labels were given before it and the annotator reviewed and kept them rather than judging those documents again, which matters most for the two slices where they dominate (12 of 14 and 11 of 17).
The single-coder design does not measure agreement on ambiguous Czech/Slovak text.
Among the 25 documents drawn per agent finding, at least 18 hosts are
represented and no host contributes more than 16%.
Validation measures precision only. We do not know the recall of any selector, so the
tests guard specific patterns and do not show that they capture contamination
broadly. Our defect criterion (not Slovak or junk) is coarse, and we do not measure
downstream language-model effects ( Artetxe et al., 2022 ) .

blocks.en: Ethical Considerations
blocks.zh: 道德考虑

blocks.en:
The corpus is public web text redistributed under ODC-By, and we report aggregate
statistics and short excerpts only. Several discovered slices consist of adult
spam. The corpus release already flags profanity-list matches, and we neither
reproduce such content in the paper nor include it in the released examples
beyond what is necessary to document the finding. The annotation task required a
native speaker to read web text that includes such material. Before the task began,
the annotator was told to expect explicit content and that any document could be
skipped and the work stopped at any time.
Released excerpts and trajectories are redacted for third-party personal
data. Real email addresses are replaced with a marker at the tool boundary, while
the corpus’s own anonymisation placeholders are kept, since one candidate finding
concerns them. The placeholders appear in 3.74% of sampled documents against
0.009% carrying an address that survived the pipeline’s scrubbing, so
FineWeb2’s anonymisation is close to complete and we do not republish the residue.

blocks.en:
System prompt (verbatim) You are a careful empirical researcher
auditing a large text corpus that was built
automatically from web crawls. You interact
with the corpus only through the provided
tools. You cannot see the corpus any other
way, and you cannot modify it.

The corpus under audit is one language-
specific slice of a large multilingual web
corpus. Its curation pipeline labelled every
document in it as Slovak (‘slk_Latn‘),
applied quality heuristics, and deduplicated
it. The slice is intended to be used as
pretraining data for language models and as
a linguistic resource for Slovak.

Your job is to find out, empirically, in
what ways this slice fails to be what it
claims to be, and to leave behind machine-
checkable evidence of each failure you can
substantiate.

# What counts as a finding

A finding is a *systematic* property of a
*coherent subset* of documents that makes
those documents wrong, misleading, or
unusable given what the corpus claims to be.
It must be:

1. **Systematic** -- it recurs across
   documents, hosts, or crawls; a single
   strange document is not a finding.
2. **Reproducibly retrievable** -- you can
   write a SQL condition over the available
   columns (optionally using the text) that
   selects the affected documents with
   reasonable precision.
3. **Grounded** -- you have actually
   inspected documents that the condition
   selects, and you know what the condition
   wrongly catches.
4. **Quantified** -- you have measured how
   much of the corpus it affects.

Do not invent categories a priori and go
looking for them. Start from what the data
actually shows: distributions, outliers,
structure across hosts and crawls, and
documents you have read. Let the corpus
tell you what is wrong with it.

# How to work

Iterate, and be explicit at each step:

1. Orient: look at the schema and at
   aggregate structure.
2. Form a specific hypothesis about a
   defect, stated so that it could be
   wrong.
3. Retrieve targeted evidence *and*
   counter-evidence. Look at documents
   that should be affected and documents
   that should not.
4. Refine or reject the hypothesis.
   Rejecting a hypothesis on evidence is a
   good outcome; say so and move on.
5. Estimate prevalence with
   ‘run_detector‘.
6. Where the phenomenon admits it,
   synthesise a cheap selector, check its
   precision yourself with
   ‘evaluate_detector‘, and record it with
   ‘save_finding‘, including what it
   wrongly catches.

# Constraints

* You have a strict budget of document
  inspections, shown by ‘schema‘ and after
  each inspecting call. Spend it
  deliberately: aggregates are free,
  reading documents is not. Reserve
  budget for checking your candidate
  selectors, not only for exploring.
* Aim for a small number of strong,
  distinct findings rather than many weak
  ones. Do not split one phenomenon into
  arbitrary variants; one finding per
  phenomenon, with the best selector you
  can write.
* A selector that only uses metadata
  columns can be measured exactly on the
  whole corpus, which is more useful than
  one that needs the text. Prefer cheap
  selectors when they are about as
  accurate.
* Be calibrated. When you record a
  finding, your ‘expected_precision‘
  should be your honest estimate from the
  documents you inspected, and your
  ‘evidence‘ field should state what you
  checked, including anything that argues
  against the finding.
* Never claim a measurement you did not
  make.

Work autonomously until your inspection
budget is nearly exhausted or you have no
further productive hypotheses. Then stop
and summarise: the findings you recorded,
the hypotheses you rejected and why, and
what you would investigate next with more
budget.

blocks.en:
This appendix tests whether the written tests and the framework carry over to other
languages, not whether the agent discovers defects there, as we ran no agent on them.
Nothing in the framework is Slovak except the tests, so we pointed it at the test shards of eleven other FineWeb2 configurations, plus FineWeb2’s own
Slovak (our corpus is a redistribution of it with extra columns). Upstream ships
fewer columns, lacking the auxiliary LID predictions and the profanity count, which
is the situation a second language community is actually in. The adapter
materialises absent columns as NULL and says so, and the runner then refuses to
score a test it cannot measure. On upstream Slovak, five of the seven slice guards
are therefore reported unmeasurable instead of passing at zero prevalence, which
would have been the dangerous outcome. The two that survive on metadata alone
reproduce there, the content farm at 3.72% and the machine-translation farm at
0.258%, so those slices come from FineWeb2, not the redistributor. On the
11 foreign corpora all seven Slovak tests are correctly reported out of
scope, and the two language-neutral invariants run. Identifier uniqueness passes
everywhere, and the invalid-confidence invariant fails in 11 of 12 configurations
(Table 5 ), with Swahili the one clean configuration at a
maximum score of 0.99990. The shares vary by a factor of thirty-five, but the
ceiling barely moves, and it has a mechanical cause.
fastText avoids log ⁡ 0 \log 0 by computing log ⁡ ( p + 10 − 5 ) \log(p+10^{-5}) , so a maximally confident
label is reported as p + 10 − 5 p+10^{-5} . The maximum we observe equals float32 ( 1.00001 ) (1.00001) in 8 of the 11 affected configurations and lies within 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} of it in the other three (Amharic, Welsh and Hebrew). The pipeline’s language filter stores that number
unchanged, which makes the defect an upstream convention faithfully passed through
rather than a mistake in any one language. Although it leaves every document intact,
it matters to a consumer who reads the field as a probability, for instance to
re-threshold with FineWeb2’s per-language cutoffs or to average it as a confidence.
The fix is one line: clamp the score, or subtract the epsilon before publishing it.

blocks.en:
Findings compile into two kinds of test. Prevalence guards fail if
a slice grows in a future release, and invariants fail if a condition
occurs at all. A guard’s bound, 1.2 times the measured prevalence, is calibrated for
corpus-wide evaluation. Over a narrow slice of crawls the same bound is easily
exceeded by ordinary variation (2 of the seven guards over the eight newest
snapshots, all seven over the single worst one), which is information about the crawl
rather than a regression. For the content farm, the guard (1.2 times 5.32%) trips on
the crawls around the peak, roughly 2022-40 to 2023-23, and not on the two newest,
which is the guard working, since the farm far exceeds its corpus-wide share there. Both kinds are released, and a failing test is a live defect,
not a broken harness. Each kind carries what makes it retraceable, and the release check
enforces this. A guard ships the auditor’s stated evidence, up to five document ids
to start from (all 32 resolve in the corpus) and the false positives it expects, while an
invariant has none of those by construction and instead ships the mechanism that
produces the violation.

Annotation guidelines (verbatim, final version) # Slovak FineWeb2 audit: annotation
# guidelines

You will see documents drawn from a
corpus that a curation pipeline labelled as
**Slovak** and shipped as pretraining data.
Documents are shown in random order; the
sampling method and the reason a document
was selected are deliberately hidden from
you.

For each document give **two** labels.

## 1. Language

* ‘sk‘      Slovak. Normal Slovak text.
            Informal, diacritic-free or
            misspelled Slovak still counts
            as Slovak.
* ‘sk-pred‘ Predominantly Slovak: mostly
            Slovak, but with a non-trivial
            amount of another language
            (e.g. a Czech or English block).
* ‘cs‘      Czech. The document is
            essentially Czech.
* ‘mix‘     Mixed Slovak/Czech:
            substantial amounts of both,
            neither clearly dominant.
* ‘other‘   Some other language, or
            genuinely multilingual beyond
            sk/cs.
* ‘?‘       Uncertain.

## 2. Usefulness as Slovak corpus text

* ‘good‘    Useful natural text: coherent
            prose a person wrote (or a
            decent translation) that you
            would keep in a Slovak corpus.
* ‘noisy‘   Usable but noisy: real
            content mixed with menus,
            repetition, formatting debris,
            or awkward machine translation.
* ‘junk‘    Boilerplate, template,
            navigation, listing spam,
            keyword salad, incoherent
            machine-generated text, or
            otherwise not usable.
* ‘?‘       Uncertain.

Readability is not the test. Fluent,
correctly spelled Slovak is still ‘junk‘
when the page exists to place links,
keywords or advertising rather than to
say something: doorway pages, tag and
category listings, autogenerated product,
crypto or gambling copy. ‘noisy‘ is for
real content with debris around it, not
for debris that happens to be readable.

Judge only what you see. If the excerpt
is truncated, judge the excerpt.
